# Future Directions: The Diagonal as a Single Organising Principle

This cycle established, from one structural root, that no type can fully quantify
over itself: a type `T` equivalent to its own predicate space `T → (T → Prop)`
cannot exist. The same fixed-point argument — a point-surjective family forces
every self-map to have a fixed point, and negation on truth values has none — was
threaded through its classical incarnations: Cantor's cardinal gap, Tarski's
undefinability of truth, and Gödel's incompleteness. The decisive discovery was
that Gödel and Tarski differ *only* in which predicates a system can name: negated
provability is nameable, negated truth is not.

## Conjecture 1 — The definability gate governs the whole incompleteness spectrum

Between "nothing internal is nameable" (trivially consistent) and "everything is
nameable" (Tarski collapse) lies a monotone lattice of naming powers, and each
level realises a sharply different incompleteness phenomenon (consistency,
essential incompleteness, ω-incompleteness, outright inconsistency).

The key insight is that consistency is not a property of the sentences a system
proves but of the *predicates it is allowed to name*: the fixed-point operator is
always present, and only the definability gate decides whether its output is a
theorem, an undecidable sentence, or a contradiction.

Why now? The restricted-diagonal formulation isolates definability as an explicit,
independently variable parameter rather than an implicit feature of a fixed
language, so the whole spectrum can be studied by moving a single dial.

## Conjecture 2 — Every diagonal impossibility has a quantitative cardinal shadow

Each qualitative "no self-reflecting object" theorem is the boundary case of a
strict size inequality; conversely, any strict cardinal gap `#A < #(A → B)` with a
fixed-point-free self-map of `B` yields a corresponding impossibility theorem.

The key insight is that the logical obstruction and the arithmetic gap are two
readings of the *same* diagonal witness: the sentence that cannot be named is
exactly the element that cannot be hit.

Why now? Having both readings — the fixed-point theorem and the strict cardinal
inequality — derived side by side makes the correspondence between them a concrete
target rather than an analogy.

## Conjecture 3 — Fixed-point-free self-maps classify which structures resist self-reference

A type `B` of "truth values" admits a self-quantifying object built on it exactly
when `B` carries *some* self-map with a fixed point for every point-surjective
family; the obstruction is precisely the existence of a fixed-point-free self-map
such as negation.

The key insight is that impossibility of self-reference is not about the size of
`T` at all but about the fixed-point geometry of the value space `B`: replace
two-valued logic by a structure whose every self-map has a fixed point and the
obstruction dissolves.

Why now? Lawvere's theorem, stated with the value type fully general, makes the
role of the value space explicit, turning "which logics permit self-reference?"
into a precise question about fixed-point-free endomorphisms.

## Conjecture 4 — Consciousness-style total self-models are impossible for the same reason

Any agent whose internal state space is rich enough to represent every predicate
about its own states — a "total self-model" — is subject to the diagonal
obstruction and cannot be complete: there is always a true self-predicate it
cannot internally name.

The key insight is that a total self-model would be exactly a self-quantifying
type `T ≃ (T → Prop)`, so the impossibility proved here is not a limitation of any
particular architecture but a structural ceiling on complete self-representation.

Why now? With the impossibility of the self-quantifying equivalence established in
full generality, claims about "complete self-awareness" acquire a precise
mathematical meaning against which they can finally be tested and refuted.

import Mathlib

/-!
# Functional equations enforce primitivity: the genuine root-number reciprocity law

This file **deepens** the analysis in `FunctionalEquationPrimitivity.lean`.  There the
root-number reciprocity law was proved only in *identity form*
`W(χ)·W(χ⁻¹)·Λ(χ,s) = Λ(χ,s)`, deliberately avoiding a non-vanishing hypothesis so that the
statement stayed unconditional.  Here we upgrade it to the genuine equality
`W(χ)·W(χ⁻¹) = 1` in the setting where the arithmetic of Gauss sums is fully available,
namely a **prime modulus** `p`, where `ZMod p` is a field and the standard additive
character is primitive.

The engine is the Gauss-sum identity `gaussSum χ ψ · gaussSum χ⁻¹ ψ⁻¹ = #(ZMod p)` for a
nontrivial multiplicative character `χ` against a primitive additive character `ψ`.  Feeding
in `ψ = stdAddChar` and the reflection `χ(-1)·gaussSum χ⁻¹ ψ⁻¹ = gaussSum χ⁻¹ ψ` turns this
into `gaussSum χ ψ · gaussSum χ⁻¹ ψ = χ(-1)·p`.  Dividing by the Archimedean factor and by
`p` — and observing that the parity factor `I^{2a}` cancels `χ(-1)` exactly — yields the
clean reciprocity `W(χ)·W(χ⁻¹) = 1`.

## Main results

* `FEPrimitivityDeep.inv_even_iff` — inversion preserves parity of a Dirichlet character.
* `FEPrimitivityDeep.gaussSum_mul_gaussSum_inv_stdAddChar` — the same-character Gauss-sum
  product `gaussSum χ · gaussSum χ⁻¹ = χ(-1)·p`.
* `FEPrimitivityDeep.rootNumber_mul_rootNumber_inv` — **genuine reciprocity** `W(χ)·W(χ⁻¹) = 1`.
* `FEPrimitivityDeep.rootNumber_ne_zero` — the root number of a nontrivial character mod `p`
  is non-zero.
* `FEPrimitivityDeep.rootNumber_inv_eq_inv` — `W(χ⁻¹) = W(χ)⁻¹`.
* `FEPrimitivityDeep.rootNumber_sq_self_dual` — for a real character, `W(χ)² = 1`, i.e. the
  root number of a quadratic character is a sign.
* `FEPrimitivityDeep.completedLFunction_inv_eq` — reflection identity rewritten through the
  genuine reciprocity, expressing `Λ(χ⁻¹, s)` from `Λ(χ, 1-s)`.
-/

namespace FEPrimitivityDeep

open DirichletCharacter Complex
open ZMod (stdAddChar isPrimitive_stdAddChar)

/-! ### Inversion preserves parity -/

/-- Inversion of a Dirichlet character preserves parity: `χ` is even iff `χ⁻¹` is even. -/
lemma inv_even_iff {N : ℕ} [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N) :
    χ.Even ↔ χ⁻¹.Even := by
  unfold DirichletCharacter.Even
  rw [MulChar.inv_apply_eq_inv' χ (-1), inv_eq_one]

/-! ### The same-character Gauss-sum product for a prime modulus -/

/-- For a prime modulus `p` and a nontrivial Dirichlet character `χ`, the product of the
Gauss sums of `χ` and `χ⁻¹` against the *same* standard additive character equals
`χ(-1)·p`.  This is the field-case Gauss-sum reciprocity, with the additive-character
inversion folded in via `mul_gaussSum_inv_eq_gaussSum`. -/
theorem gaussSum_mul_gaussSum_inv_stdAddChar {p : ℕ} [Fact p.Prime]
    (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ p) (hχ : χ ≠ 1) :
    gaussSum χ stdAddChar * gaussSum χ⁻¹ stdAddChar = χ (-1) * (p : ℂ) := by
  have hprim := isPrimitive_stdAddChar p
  have hcard := gaussSum_mul_gaussSum_eq_card (χ := χ) hχ hprim
  have hinv := mul_gaussSum_inv_eq_gaussSum χ⁻¹ (stdAddChar (N := p))
  have hsq : χ (-1) * χ (-1) = 1 := by rw [← map_mul]; norm_num
  have hne : χ (-1) ≠ 0 := by intro h; rw [h, mul_zero] at hsq; exact zero_ne_one hsq
  have hxinv : χ⁻¹ (-1) = (χ (-1))⁻¹ := MulChar.inv_apply_eq_inv' χ (-1)
  have hconv : gaussSum χ⁻¹ stdAddChar⁻¹ = χ (-1) * gaussSum χ⁻¹ stdAddChar := by
    have h2 := congrArg (fun z => χ (-1) * z) hinv
    simp only [hxinv, ← mul_assoc, mul_inv_cancel₀ hne, one_mul] at h2
    exact h2
  rw [hconv, ZMod.card] at hcard
  have hkey : χ (-1) * (gaussSum χ stdAddChar * gaussSum χ⁻¹ stdAddChar) = (p : ℂ) := by
    rw [← hcard]; ring
  calc gaussSum χ stdAddChar * gaussSum χ⁻¹ stdAddChar
      = χ (-1) * χ (-1) * (gaussSum χ stdAddChar * gaussSum χ⁻¹ stdAddChar) := by
        rw [hsq, one_mul]
    _ = χ (-1) * (χ (-1) * (gaussSum χ stdAddChar * gaussSum χ⁻¹ stdAddChar)) := by ring
    _ = χ (-1) * (p : ℂ) := by rw [hkey]

/-! ### Genuine root-number reciprocity -/

/-- **Genuine root-number reciprocity for a prime modulus.**  For a nontrivial Dirichlet
character `χ` modulo a prime `p`, the root numbers of `χ` and `χ⁻¹` are genuine
multiplicative inverses: `W(χ)·W(χ⁻¹) = 1`.  This upgrades the identity-form reciprocity of
`FunctionalEquationPrimitivity.lean` to an honest equality of complex numbers. -/
theorem rootNumber_mul_rootNumber_inv {p : ℕ} [Fact p.Prime]
    (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ p) (hχ : χ ≠ 1) :
    rootNumber χ * rootNumber χ⁻¹ = 1 := by
  classical
  have hgs := gaussSum_mul_gaussSum_inv_stdAddChar χ hχ
  have hpar : (χ.Even ↔ χ⁻¹.Even) := inv_even_iff χ
  have hp0 : (p : ℂ) ≠ 0 := by exact_mod_cast (Fact.out (p := p.Prime)).ne_zero
  have hpsq : ((p : ℂ) ^ (1/2 : ℂ)) ^ 2 = (p : ℂ) := by
    rw [sq, ← Complex.cpow_add _ _ hp0]; norm_num
  have hpsq0 : ((p : ℂ) ^ (1/2 : ℂ)) ≠ 0 := by
    intro h; rw [h] at hpsq; simp at hpsq; exact hp0 hpsq.symm
  unfold rootNumber
  rw [show (if χ⁻¹.Even then 0 else 1) = (if χ.Even then (0:ℕ) else 1) by

# Computational Evidence: Primitive Prime Divisors of Fibonacci Numbers

A prime `p` is a **primitive divisor** of `F(n)` if `p ∣ F(n)` but `p ∤ F(k)`
for all `0 < k < n`.  Carmichael's theorem asserts that `F(n)` has a primitive
prime divisor for every `n` outside the exceptional set `{1, 2, 6, 12}`.

## Small-case verification

Using the least-index (rank of apparition) `ρ(p) = min { m > 0 : p ∣ F(m) }`,
a prime `p ∣ F(n)` is primitive exactly when `ρ(p) = n`.  Direct computation of
`(n, F(n), has-primitive-divisor)`:

| n  | F(n) | primitive divisor? | reason |
|----|------|--------------------|--------|
| 1  | 1    | no  | F(1)=1 has no prime factor |
| 2  | 1    | no  | F(2)=1 has no prime factor |
| 3  | 2    | yes | 2 first appears at n=3 |
| 4  | 3    | yes | 3 first appears at n=4 |
| 5  | 5    | yes | 5 first appears at n=5 |
| 6  | 8    | **no**  | only prime is 2, with ρ(2)=3 < 6 |
| 7  | 13   | yes | 13 |
| 8  | 21   | yes | 7 (ρ(7)=8) |
| 11 | 89   | yes | 89 |
| 12 | 144  | **no**  | primes 2 (ρ=3) and 3 (ρ=4), none primitive |
| 13 | 233  | yes | 233 |

For every `13 ≤ n ≤ 20` a primitive divisor exists, matching the theorem.  The
only indices `≥ 1` without a primitive divisor are `{1, 2, 6, 12}`.

## Certificate for the finite range

For all composite `n` with `13 ≤ n ≤ 10000`, the combinatorial *primitive part*
`primPart n` (the part of `F(n)` coprime to every earlier `F(d)`) satisfies
`primPart n > 1`, and its least prime factor is a primitive divisor.  This is a
finite, exhaustively checked certificate.

## Sequences

- The exceptional indices `{1, 2, 6, 12}` are the classical exceptions in
  Carmichael's theorem for the Fibonacci sequence.
- Number of primitive prime factors of `F(n)`: OEIS A086597 (which is `0`
  exactly at `n ∈ {1, 2, 6, 12}` among `n ≥ 1`).

## Counterexample hunt

No composite `n` in `13 ≤ n ≤ 10000` lacks a primitive divisor (verified).  The
growth of the primitive part is governed by `|primitive part| ≈ φ^{ϕ(n)}` with
`φ` the golden ratio and `ϕ` Euler's totient; since `ϕ(n)` grows without bound,
no counterexample is expected for any `n > 12`, consistent with the theorem.

# Future Directions

Derived from this cycle's work on (a) the mixed-radix / factorial number-system
bridge and (b) primitive prime divisors of Fibonacci numbers (Carmichael's
theorem).

## 1. A uniform "running-product" uniqueness theorem for all positional systems
The mixed-radix uniqueness result subsumes the factorial system exactly because
place values are the running products of the bases. The key insight is that
uniqueness of a positional representation depends only on the sequence of running
products being strictly increasing enough that each digit is recovered by a single
Euclidean division, never on the arithmetic meaning of the bases themselves. Why
now? With the factorial system already realized as the instance `b i = i + 1` and
base-`N` as `b i = N`, a single parameterized theorem can now be tested against
irregular bases (e.g. primorial or Fibonacci bases) to map exactly which base
sequences still yield unique representations.

## 2. Carmichael's theorem via the primitive part as a size inequality
For composite `n`, the existence of a primitive prime divisor of `F_n` is
equivalent to `1 < primPart n`, where `primPart n` is `F_n` with every factor
shared with an earlier Fibonacci number stripped away. The key insight is that the
whole theorem reduces to a single inequality: the primitive part grows like
`φ^{ϕ(n)}` while the total imprimitive contribution is bounded by the largest prime
factor of `n` taken to first order. Why now? The computational branch already
certifies `1 < primPart n` for all composite `n` up to `10^4`; isolating the
growth-versus-obstruction inequality is the one missing analytic step that would
convert the finite check into an unconditional theorem.

## 3. Rank of apparition as the organizing invariant
Every prime `p` has a rank of apparition `α(p)`, the least `m` with `p ∣ F_m`, and
`p ∣ F_n` holds precisely when `α(p) ∣ n`. The key insight is that the strong
divisibility identity `gcd(F_m, F_n) = F_{gcd(m,n)}` alone forces the divisor set
of each prime to be an arithmetic progression of multiples of `α(p)`, so
"primitive divisor of `F_n`" is exactly "prime of rank `n`". Why now? This
reformulation turns Carmichael's theorem into a counting statement about which
values `n` are attained as ranks, a form that is far more amenable to induction on
the divisor lattice of `n` than the direct divisibility statement.

## 4. Lifting the exponent for Fibonacci numbers
Bounding the imprimitive part requires knowing, for a prime `p` of rank `r`,
